title: 📘 UNIT 3: PEOPLES, STATES AND HISTORICAL PROCESSES IN ETHIOPIA AND THE HORN TO THE END OF THE 13TH CENTURY
notes:
The Horn of Africa → Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia.

The region is one of the important areas of early human evolution and the development of ancient cultures and states.

Ethiopia → highly diverse in peoples, languages, religions and ways of life.

Major historical themes → settlement of peoples + language and religion + trade + state formation + cultural interaction.

title: 3.1 🗣️ Languages, Religions and Peoples of Ethiopia and the Horn
notes:
Ethiopia has more than 85 languages belonging mainly to four language families:

• Cushitic → Oromo, Afar, Somali, Sidama, Hadiya, Kambata, Gedeo and others.
• Omotic → Wolaita, Gamo, Gofa, Dawuro, Kafa, Ari, Dizi and others.
• Semitic → Amharic, Tigrigna, Tigre, Ge'ez, Guraghe, Harari, Argoba, Silti and others.
• Nilo-Saharan → Anuak, Nuer, Berta, Gumuz, Majang, Komo and others.

📌 Ethiopia's linguistic diversity reflects long-term migration, settlement and interaction among peoples.

title: 3.1.1 🔤 Language Families and Their Distribution
notes:
Cushitic peoples → widely distributed across northern, central, eastern and southern Ethiopia and the Horn.

Omotic peoples → mainly concentrated in southwestern Ethiopia, especially around the Omo River basin. Shinasha and South Mao are important exceptions.

Semitic peoples → concentrated mainly in the northern and central highlands but also spread to other areas.

Nilo-Saharan peoples → mainly found in western Ethiopia along the Ethio-Sudan border, with some groups extending toward the southern Omo region.

📜 Ge'ez → ancient indigenous Ethiopian language and writing tradition that became important in literature, religion and historical records.

title: 3.1.2 🙏 Religions of Ethiopia and the Horn
notes:
Three major monotheistic religions became established in Ethiopia:
• Judaism.
• Christianity.
• Islam.

Before their introduction, different communities practiced indigenous religions.

Indigenous religions commonly included belief in a supreme creator and spiritual beings, although practices and names differed among peoples.

title: 3.1.2.1 🌿 Indigenous Religions
notes:
Waqefanna → indigenous Oromo religion.

Waqa → supreme creator and source of life.
Ayyana → manifestations/expressions of Waqa's creative power.
Qallu/Qalliti → religious specialists who performed important religious functions.
Abba Muda → important spiritual leader among the Oromo.
Jila → ceremony connecting the spiritual leadership with the Oromo community.

Other Ethiopian peoples also developed their own indigenous religious traditions.

title: 3.1.2.2 ✡️ Judaism and the Bete-Israel
notes:
Judaism → one of the early monotheistic traditions associated with Ethiopia.

Traditional accounts connect Ethiopian Jews with the story of the Queen of Sheba, King Solomon and Menelik I, while other traditions explain their presence through ancient migrations.

Bete-Israel → Ethiopian Jewish community with its own religious, social and cultural traditions.

📌 Their historical communities were concentrated especially in areas such as Wogera, Quara, Tegede, Welqayt and Simen.

title: 3.1.2.3 ✝️ Christianity in Ethiopia
notes:
Christianity was introduced into Aksum during the 4th century A.D.

👤 Frumentius → played the central role in introducing Christianity to King Ezana and became the first bishop of Ethiopia.

👑 Ezana → accepted Christianity; Christian symbols later appeared on his coins and inscriptions.

👤 Nine Saints → helped spread Christianity and monasticism beyond the royal court.

Major contributions → translation of religious texts into Ge'ez + church literature + religious art + architecture + liturgy.

👤 Saint Yared → famous for developing Ethiopian Orthodox church music, hymns and liturgical traditions.

title: 3.1.2.4 ☪️ Islam in Ethiopia and the Horn
notes:
Islam reached Ethiopia very early through the first Muslim migration to Aksum in 615 A.D.

👤 Prophet Muhammad → directed some of his followers to seek refuge in Ethiopia because the Aksumite king was known for justice and protection.

👤 Ja'far ibn Abi Talib → led the early Muslim refugees to the Aksumite kingdom.

The Aksumite king protected the refugees and refused to hand them over to their opponents.

Later spread of Islam → Red Sea trade + Muslim merchants + migration + peaceful preaching.

Important routes → Dahlak Islands and Zeila, with Zeila becoming especially important for the spread of Islam into the interior.

title: 3.1.3 🏘️ Settlement of Peoples
notes:
Settlement pattern → distribution of peoples across a geographical area.

It was shaped by:
• Environment and climate.
• Economic activities.
• Migration.
• Political expansion.
• Warfare and state formation.
• Interaction among neighboring peoples.

Cushitic and Semitic peoples → spread across large parts of northern, northeastern, central, eastern and southern Ethiopia.

Omotic peoples → mainly settled in southwestern Ethiopia around the Omo basin.

Nilotic peoples → mainly settled along the Ethio-Sudan border and western lowlands.

📌 Settlement patterns changed continuously through historical processes.

title: 3.2 🏺 Pre-Aksumite States and Their Geographical Setting
notes:
Important pre-Aksumite centers → Punt and Da'amat.

These states demonstrate that organized political communities, agriculture, trade and cultural interaction existed in the Horn before the rise of Aksum.

title: 3.2.1 🚢 Punt
notes:
Punt → earliest historically known state in the Horn of Africa according to Egyptian written records.

📜 Main evidence → Egyptian records describing naval expeditions to Punt.

👑 Pharaoh Sahure (c.2743–2731 B.C.) → sent an expedition to obtain myrrh, ebony and electrum.

👑 Queen Hatshepsut (c.1490–1468 B.C.) → organized the best-documented Egyptian expedition to Punt; the expedition is depicted at Deir el-Bahri.

Punt exported → frankincense, myrrh, spices, sandalwood, ivory, animal skins, ostrich feathers and eggs, monkeys, giraffes, gold and other products.

Egypt exported → axes, daggers, swords, knives, sickles, clothing, bracelets, necklaces and beads.

📍 Exact location remains uncertain. Proposed areas include northern/northeastern Somalia, northern Ethiopia and the Red Sea region.

title: 3.2.2 🏛️ Da'amat
notes:
Da'amat → first historically known state in Ethiopia according to the textbook.

Period → approximately 980–400 B.C.
Capital → Yeha, about 30 km northeast of Aksum.

Yeha → probably began as a commercial center around 1000 B.C. and later developed into a political and cultural center.

Economic activities → agriculture + trade + livestock + metalworking.

Trade connections → especially with South Arabian merchants and Red Sea networks.

Important products → ivory, rhinoceros horn and other commodities from the interior.

📜 Writing → early inscriptions used a Sabean-related script; the script gradually developed toward the indigenous Ge'ez writing system.

title: 3.2.3 🔤 Early Ethiopian Writing, Calendar and Numerals
notes:
Sabean inscriptions → early inscriptions in the region often lacked vowels.

By the 1st century A.D. → the Ge'ez alphabet had developed.

Ge'ez script → written from left to right and became a major foundation of Ethiopian literature, religious texts and historical writing.

Ethiopian calendar → solar calendar with 12 months of 30 days plus 5 or 6 additional days.

📅 New Year → normally September 11 in the Gregorian calendar, with September 12 occurring before a Gregorian leap year.

Numerals → appeared in Ethiopia and the Horn by the beginning of the 4th century A.D.

title: 3.3 👑 The Aksumite Kingdom
notes:
Aksum → developed into one of the most powerful ancient states of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region.

Period of major importance → roughly 1st–7th centuries A.D.

📍 Center → northern Ethiopia and Eritrea.
📍 Adulis → major port and commercial center.

Aksum became a major political, economic, cultural and religious power and was recognized as one of the four great powers of its time together with Rome, Persia and China.

title: 3.3.1 🌾 Economic Foundations of Aksum
notes:
Aksum's economy was based mainly on:
• Agriculture.
• Livestock.
• Local crafts.
• Long-distance trade.
• Maritime commerce.

📍 Adulis → connected Aksum to Red Sea, Arabian, Mediterranean and Indian Ocean trade.

Major exports → ivory, gold, spices, frankincense, myrrh, animal products and slaves.

Major imports → textiles, glassware, jewelry, metal products, oil, wine and other manufactured goods.

Aksumite rulers → minted gold, silver and bronze coins for local and international transactions.

title: 3.3.2 🚢 Aksum and International Trade
notes:
Aksum maintained commercial and diplomatic contacts with:
• South Arabia.
• Roman/Byzantine world.
• Persia.
• India.
• Ceylon (Sri Lanka).
• Mediterranean regions.

👤 Zoscales (c.76–89 A.D.) → Aksumite king known for knowledge of Greek and overseas trade.

👤 Gadarat → Aksumite ruler associated with military activities across the Red Sea around the early 3rd century.

📜 Adulis inscription → important evidence for Aksum's trade and external relations.

🚢 Aksum → developed shipbuilding technology and maintained a fleet used for both trade and warfare.

title: 3.3.3 ✝️ Christianity and the Aksumite Kingdom
notes:
Christianity entered the Aksumite royal court during the 4th century.

👤 Frumentius → converted King Ezana and became the first bishop of Ethiopia.

👑 Ezana → adopted Christianity and used Christian symbols in inscriptions and coinage.

Christianity gradually became an important institution in Aksumite political and cultural life.

👑 Kaleb (c.500–535 A.D.) → expanded Aksumite influence across the Red Sea and intervened in Himyar.

👑 Gebre Mesqel → succeeded Kaleb.

👤 Yared → developed important Ethiopian Orthodox liturgical songs and hymns during this period.

title: 3.3.4 🗿 Aksumite Achievements
notes:
Major achievements:
• Gold, silver and bronze coinage.
• Ge'ez writing system.
• Inscriptions and historical records.
• Large stone stelae/obelisks.
• Advanced stone construction.
• Calendar and numerals.
• Shipbuilding.
• Long-distance maritime trade.
• Christian religious architecture.
• Literature and artistic traditions.

📌 Aksumite stelae → monumental stone structures showing advanced engineering and artistic skill.

📌 Ge'ez → became an important language of religion, literature and historical documentation.

title: 3.3.5 ⚔️ Aksum and South Arabia
notes:
Aksum's Red Sea position created both trade and conflict with South Arabian states.

Aksumite rulers sometimes intervened militarily across the Red Sea.

👑 Kaleb → fought against Dhu-Nuwas of Himyar after Christians in the region were persecuted.

With Byzantine support, Kaleb defeated Dhu-Nuwas and appointed Abraha as governor.

📌 These events demonstrate the political and religious importance of Aksum's Red Sea connections.

title: 3.3.6 📉 Decline of Aksum
notes:
Aksum began to decline from the late 7th century due to several internal and external pressures.

Major factors:
• Environmental degradation.
• Decline in agricultural productivity.
• Possible plague.
• Increasing political and military pressure.
• Arab expansion around the Red Sea.
• Destruction of Adulis around 702 A.D.
• Loss of important maritime trade routes.

📌 Destruction of Adulis → severely damaged Aksum's economic connection with international trade.

The decline was gradual rather than the result of a single event.

title: 3.4 ☪️ The Sultanate of Shewa
notes:
Sultanate → Muslim state ruled by a sultan who exercised political and religious authority.

Sultanate of Shewa → one of the earliest Muslim sultanates in the Ethiopian region.

📍 Territory → roughly from northeastern Shewa toward northern Hararghe.
📅 Founded → around 896 A.D.
👤 First known ruler → Khalid ibn al-Walid.
👑 Dynasty → Makhzumite, claiming descent from the Makhzumi clan of South Arabia.
📍 Capital → Walele in northern Hararghe.

title: 3.4.1 ⚔️ Shewa, Damot and Ifat
notes:
The Sultanate of Shewa frequently fought the Kingdom of Damot, which weakened Shewa.

During the 13th century → Damot extended its influence over Shewa.

The Sultanate of Ifat → expanded east of Shewa and repeatedly campaigned against the Makhzumite rulers.

1285 A.D. → Walasma dynasty of Ifat overthrew the Makhzumite dynasty.

📌 Result → the independent Sultanate of Shewa came to an end.

title: 3.5 ⛪ The Zagwe Dynasty
notes:
Zagwe Dynasty → ruled approximately from the mid-12th century to 1270.

Founder → Mera Tekle Haymanot.

According to the textbook → Mera Tekle Haymanot was originally a general associated with Dil Na'od and later established the Zagwe ruling family.

📍 Power base → Lasta.
📍 Political center → Adafa near Roha (Lalibela), in the Bugna area of Wag and Lasta.

The Zagwe kingdom covered much of the former Aksumite highlands, extending toward northern Shewa and the Lake Tana/Gojjam region.

title: 3.5.1 🔄 Continuity with Aksum
notes:
The Zagwe rulers maintained many Aksumite traditions.

Continuities included:
• Christianity.
• Ge'ez literary tradition.
• Political and cultural traditions.
• Trade connections.
• Christian architecture.

The Zagwe also renewed trade and cultural contacts with the eastern Mediterranean.

Major exports → ivory, spices and slaves.
Major imports → cotton, linen, silver and copper vessels, and newly minted coins.

title: 3.5.2 🏛️ Achievements of the Zagwe Period
notes:
Major achievements:
• Rock-hewn churches.
• Religious paintings.
• Translation of religious works from Arabic into Ge'ez.
• Development of Christian architecture.
• Continued literary traditions.
• Trade with the eastern Mediterranean.

👑 Lalibela → most famous Zagwe ruler associated with the development of the rock-hewn churches.

⛪ Bete Giyorgis → monolithic church carved in the shape of a cross.

📌 Lalibela churches → registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.

title: 3.5.3 ✝️ Lalibela and the 'Second Jerusalem'
notes:
Muslim control of important Red Sea routes made travel by Ethiopian Christian pilgrims to Jerusalem more difficult.

👑 Lalibela → attempted to establish a symbolic 'Second Jerusalem' in Ethiopia.

The rock-hewn churches were therefore not only architectural achievements but also connected to religious and pilgrimage purposes.

📌 The churches were carved directly from rock, including cave, semi-hewn and monolithic structures.

title: 3.5.4 🔄 End of the Zagwe Dynasty
notes:
Main causes:
• Internal royal succession problems.
• Opposition from groups claiming descent from the ancient Aksumite rulers.
• Political claims based on the Solomonic tradition.

👤 Yekuno-Amlak (r.1270–1285) → claimed descent from Dil Na'od, the last Aksumite king.

👤 Yetbarek → last Zagwe ruler.

1270 → Yekuno-Amlak defeated Yetbarek and took power.

📌 Result → end of the Zagwe period and restoration of the Solomonic dynasty.

title: 3.6 🏹 The Kingdom of Damot
notes:
Damot → powerful medieval kingdom located south of the Abay (Blue Nile) River.

Damot was strong enough to:
• Force the Sultanate of Shewa to pay tribute.
• Defeat armies sent by the Zagwe dynasty.
• Conquer several Muslim and Christian territories.

The growth of Damot's power caused concern among neighboring states.

title: 3.6.1 ⚔️ Damot and Other States
notes:
Damot had important relationships with:
• Sultanate of Shewa.
• Zagwe Kingdom.
• Christian kingdom under Yekuno-Amlak.
• Muslim communities and territories.

Shewa and the new Christian state under Yekuno-Amlak formed an alliance to counter Damot's influence.

14th century → King Amda Tsiyon subdued Damot.

Afterward → Damot remained under the influence of the Solomonic kingdom.

title: 3.6.2 🧭 Damot and Population Movement
notes:
Later Oromo population movement and expansion affected the settlement of Damot's people.

During the late 16th and early 17th centuries → some Damot people were forced to move north of the Abay.

📍 New settlement area → southern Gojjam.

📌 Population movements changed the geographical distribution of peoples and contributed to new cultural and political interactions.

title: 3.7 ✡️ The Bete-Israel (Ethiopian Jews)
notes:
Bete-Israel → Ethiopian Jewish community with a distinct religious and cultural identity.

The textbook also discusses them in relation to occupational specialization.

Occupational castes → communities marginalized because occupations such as pottery, blacksmithing and leatherworking were considered low-status by sections of the wider society.

📍 Historical Bete-Israel communities → Wogera, Quara, Tegede, Welqayt and Simen.

title: 3.7.1 ⚔️ Bete-Israel and the Christian Kingdom
notes:
Relations between the Bete-Israel and the Christian Highland Kingdom were not always peaceful.

Main sources of conflict → religious pressure + political pressure + economic pressure.

1413–1478 → pressure increased from gradual encroachment to large-scale conflicts.

👑 King Yishaq → conquered Bete-Israel communities in Wogera around 1413.

Yishaq's decree → those who accepted baptism could inherit their father's land; those who refused were deprived of inheritance rights and associated with the term 'Felasi'.

📌 Loss of land rights encouraged Bete-Israel communities to develop specialized occupations for survival.

title: 3.7.2 🔨 Bete-Israel Skills and Economic Contributions
notes:
Important skills included:
• Blacksmithing.
• Pottery.
• Leatherworking.
• Building.
• Other handicrafts.

👑 Zera Ya'iqob (r.1434–1468) → some Bete-Israel blacksmiths travelled with the royal court.

After 1540 → their building skills became increasingly important.

Structures associated with their work are found in places such as Guzara, Gorgora and Azezo.

📌 Their specialized skills made them economically important despite social marginalization.

title: 3.7.3 📖 Bete-Israel Religious and Social Identity
notes:
Despite political and economic pressure, Bete-Israel maintained strong religious and social identity.

📚 Te'ezaza Senbet → one of their important religious texts.

Religious practices and traditions included:
• Saturday Sabbath.
• Circumcision.
• Dietary rules.

They maintained a significant degree of social separation while preserving their religious traditions.

title: 3.7.4 🛡️ Bete-Israel Resistance and Loss of Independence
notes:
From the reign of Zera Ya'iqob onward → Bete-Israel repeatedly attempted to preserve their political independence.

They supported:
• Rebellious governors.
• Imam Ahmad Bin Ibrahim al-Ghazi.
• Rebel claimants to the throne.

Their resistance continued for generations.

👑 King Suseneyos → eventually crushed their resistance and ended their political independence.
